Section 1

What changes in operations and service at Level 5

Who it is for. For people who lead an operations, customer service or administration function: contact centre, service desk, complaints, fulfilment, field service, facilities and back-office managers and team leaders.

In an operations or service department, AI and automation arrive at the front of the queue first. An AI agent answers first-line queries. Automated ticket routing decides which team a case reaches. Drafted replies, call summaries and case notes appear before an adviser types a word. Scheduling tools propose the roster and the order of a field engineer's visits.

What changes for the department is where its people spend their effort. Simple, repeated contacts leave the queue. What reaches a person is harder, more emotional or more unusual. Team leaders check machine output as well as people's work. Quality monitoring can cover every contact rather than a sample. The knowledge base becomes something the automation reads, so one wrong article gives many wrong answers.

The learner leads that shift for their own function. They decide what the department should automate and what it should keep human. They decide how its people's roles change. They work from the department's own queue, case and order data, with the people whose work changes. The organisation's service strategy is set elsewhere and is outside this qualification.

The same qualification. A learner on this version is assessed against the same criteria, to the same assessment model, as a learner on the generic Diploma. Only the context differs. Their own department is the evidence.

Section 3

The rules operations and service works within

A department changing its work stays inside these. The learner records each one where the units ask for constraints and obligations, and works within it.

UK GDPR. Customer records, call recordings and case notes are personal data, read alongside the Data Protection Act 2018. Article 22 restricts solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. AI monitoring of colleagues' calls processes their data too. Recorded as a constraint at AU-05 1.4, and as checks and human decisions at AU-05 5.1 and PJ-05 4.4.

Equality Act 2010. A service provider must make reasonable adjustments for disabled customers. So an AI agent or automated channel cannot be the only way in. Recorded at AU-05 1.4, and as a route to a person in the fallbacks at AU-05 5.1 and PJ-05 4.5. The employer's duty to colleagues shapes the support set at EI-05 4.4.

Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The employer must protect the health and safety of employees and others affected by the work. Automated job allocation in field service, warehouse or facilities work can change who works alone and where. Recorded as a constraint at AU-05 1.4 and as a risk at AU-05 5.2 and PJ-05 4.6.

Working Time Regulations 1998. Automated rostering must still give the rest breaks and keep within the limits these regulations set. Recorded as an obligation at PJ-05 1.6 and as a check on any rostering change at AU-05 5.1.

Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992. Proposed redundancies on a large enough scale bring collective consultation duties under this Act. That duty sits with the organisation, not the department. The learner records it at EI-05 1.5 and works within it at EI-05 3.6.

Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations 2003. Automated calls, texts and emails that carry marketing fall under these regulations. Adding promotional content to service messages, such as appointment reminders, is recorded as a constraint at AU-05 1.4.

FCA Handbook, Dispute Resolution: Complaints sourcebook (DISP). Applies only to financial services firms under FCA rules. There it governs how complaints are handled and recorded. Automating complaint logging or first responses in that sector is recorded at AU-05 1.4 and PJ-05 1.6.

ZFF-GM-05

Leading a Department Through a Change in Required Capability

Level5TQT60 hoursCredits6GLH24 indicativeStatusMandatoryCriteria28

In Operations and service

Here the change is what advisers, coordinators and administrators need to be good at once automation takes the routine work. Fewer people key orders or reset passwords. More people handle escalations and check what an AI agent told a customer. Others maintain knowledge articles and notice when routing goes wrong. The learner finds what the function can do now, decides what it will need, and leads people through the difference.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Know how a change in required capability affects the work of a department.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Analyse the effects on a department's work when the capabilities its roles require change, including the effect on people whose established competence is no longer what the work requires
1.2Compare different approaches to building capability in a department, and the reasoning behind each
1.3Evaluate the reasons capability-building programmes fail to change what people do at work
1.4Identify the constraints that limit what own department can change about the capability it holds, including time, budget, role definitions, agreements and the availability of learning
1.5Evaluate the different views held within own department about the change in what its people are expected to be good at, and the reasoning given for them

Applied in Operations and service

An adviser whose strength was speed on routine calls now meets only complex ones (1.1). The learner compares ways of building capability, such as floor coaching, side-by-side listening and courses (1.2). They evaluate why training often leaves the queue unchanged (1.3). Shift patterns, time off the phones and budget are constraints (1.4), and team views are weighed (1.5).

LO2
The learner will: Be able to establish what capability a department holds and what it will require.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Determine the method used to establish what capability the department holds and what it will require, and state the reasons for choosing it
2.2Establish the capabilities the department's roles currently require, and the work each of those capabilities supports
2.3Establish the capability the department currently holds, using the department's own records and evidence from work already carried out
2.4Determine the capability the department will require as its processes change, and state the reasons
2.5Analyse the difference between the capability held and the capability required, and identify where that difference carries most cost to the department
2.6Evaluate the reliability of the evidence obtained, and state how gaps were handled

Applied in Operations and service

The learner decides how to establish what the function holds and needs (2.1). An existing skills matrix is a source, not the answer. Evidence comes from quality evaluations, escalation logs, training records and handled cases (2.3). What is required follows from changing processes, such as triaging what the AI agent cannot resolve (2.2, 2.4). The learner finds where the gap costs most (2.5) and how far the evidence holds (2.6).

LO3
The learner will: Be able to determine how a department's capability difference will be closed.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Determine the criteria against which options for closing the difference will be evaluated, and state the reasons for them
3.2Identify the options available for closing each part of the difference, including developing the people already in post, changing how work is allocated, recruiting, redeploying, and obtaining capability from outside the department
3.3Interpret the cost and the benefit of each option, using figures from the department's own systems
3.4Use relevant investigation of comparable work, inside or outside own organisation, to inform the choice between options
3.5Identify a capability the department should not attempt to build, and evaluate the reasons
3.6Evaluate the options against the criteria determined at 3.1, and state which are recommended

Applied in Operations and service

The learner sets the criteria for choosing before looking at options (3.1). Options include coaching, moving work between shifts, recruiting, redeploying from a shrinking back-office queue, or buying in support (3.2). Costs come from the department's rota and queue figures (3.3). Comparable service teams inform the choice (3.4). One capability not worth building is argued (3.5) before options are evaluated (3.6).

LO4
The learner will: Be able to lead a department through a change in what its people are expected to be good at.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify the people whose expected capability changes, and state how it changes for each
4.2Consult those people about the change, and record what was raised
4.3Analyse the concerns raised, and evaluate which of them alter the recommended options
4.4Adapt the recommendation in response to what the consultation established, and state what changed
4.5State, for each person whose expected capability changes, the actions they are expected to take, the support available to them and the period over which the change applies
4.6Determine how the change in the department's capability will be evidenced in the work the department produces, and state what will count as evidence

Applied in Operations and service

The learner names each group whose expected capability changes, such as second-line advisers who will review AI drafted replies (4.1). They consult them in huddles and one-to-ones, recording by role (4.2). Concerns that change the recommendation are sorted from those that do not (4.3, 4.4). Each person gets their actions, support and period (4.5). The learner decides what will show the change took hold (4.6).

LO5
The learner will: Be able to evaluate a change in a department's capability and own method.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Evaluate the change in the department's capability against the requirement determined at 2.4, using the evidence determined at 4.6
5.2Evaluate the effect of the change on the work the department produces, using figures from the department's own systems
5.3Identify where the change did not take effect, and evaluate the reasons
5.4Evaluate how effective the method determined at 2.1 and the criteria determined at 3.1 were, giving reasons
5.5Identify what would be determined differently at the next change in the department's required capability, and the reasons

Applied in Operations and service

The learner evaluates the change against 2.4, using the evidence chosen at 4.6 (5.1). They evaluate its effect on output from the department's own systems (5.2). Where a shift kept working the old way, the reasons are evaluated (5.3). The learner reviews their own method and criteria (5.4) and what they would decide differently (5.5).

5 learning outcomes, 28 assessment criteria. The same criteria as the generic Diploma, word for word.

Evidence from Operations and service work

  • 2.1, 2.6. A method note on how capability was established across shifts and teams. It states why that method was chosen and where evidence was thin.
  • 2.3, 2.5. A capability summary from the team's own quality evaluations, escalation logs and training records. Annotations show where the gap causes repeat contacts or rework.
  • 3.1, 3.3, 3.6. An options paper that states the learner's own criteria first. It then costs coaching, redeployment and recruitment from the department's rota and queue figures.
  • 4.2, 4.3, 4.4. Consultation notes from huddles and one-to-ones, with colleagues identified by role. A dated revision of the recommendation states what changed and why.
  • 4.5. A one-page statement for each affected role, such as second-line adviser or order administrator. It sets out actions, support and the period of the change.
  • 5.1, 5.2, 5.3. An evaluation using at least one measurement taken after the change. It draws on the department's own case or quality records and states its limits.

Keeping it at Level 5

It drops to Level 4 when the learner is handed a skills matrix, a quality scorecard or a set service-level target to close the gap against. That decides 2.1 and 3.1 for them. It rises above Level 5 when the learner redesigns the organisation's service model, which is recorded at 1.4 instead.

The unit aim, level check, boundaries, assessment guidance and evidence trail are in ZFF-GM-05 on the generic Diploma, and apply here unchanged.

ZFF-EI-05

Working with the People Whose Roles Change

Level5TQT60 hoursCredits6GLH24 indicativeStatusMandatoryCriteria27

In Operations and service

In this function the roles that change are often many and alike. Advisers lose routine contacts to an AI agent. Schedulers get rosters a tool proposes. Administrators see their data entry automated. Shift work, part-time contracts and remote teams make everyone hard to reach. The learner works with all of them, including those who do not accept the change, and with the teams who depend on them.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Know how people in a department respond when their roles change.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Analyse the effects on the work of a department when the roles within it change
1.2Evaluate what is at stake for different groups of people in a department when its roles change, and the reasoning behind the positions they take
1.3Compare different approaches to working with people through a change to their roles, and the reasoning behind each
1.4Evaluate the reasons changes to roles are agreed and then not carried through in practice
1.5Identify the obligations and constraints that govern how own department may work with people whose roles change, including consultation requirements, agreements and the organisation's own procedures

Applied in Operations and service

Once simple contacts are automated, each remaining contact is longer and harder (1.1). The learner evaluates what is at stake for long-serving advisers, new starters, team leaders and quality assessors (1.2). They compare approaches to working with people through change (1.3). They evaluate why agreed changes slip back on the floor (1.4). Consultation duties, union agreements and procedures are recorded at 1.5.

LO2
The learner will: Be able to establish how a change to roles affects the people in a department.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Identify the people whose roles change and state what changes for each, and identify the people whose work depends on the roles that change
2.2Determine the method used to establish what those people raise about the change, and state the reasons for choosing it
2.3Establish, using that method, what each person or group raises about the change, and record it
2.4Analyse what was raised to establish which points concern the change itself and which concern the way it is being made
2.5Interpret what was raised to establish which parts of the change are least likely to be carried through in practice, and state the reasons
2.6Evaluate the reliability of what the method established, and state how the position of people who did not take part was handled

Applied in Operations and service

The learner identifies each changing role and who depends on it, such as the dispatch team that relies on case notes (2.1). They decide how to hear from every shift and site, and why (2.2). They record what each group raises (2.3). They separate objections to the change from objections to how it is made (2.4). They judge which parts may not hold (2.5) and how absent voices were handled (2.6).

LO3
The learner will: Be able to determine how a department will respond to people who do not accept a change.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Determine the criteria against which the department's response to each point raised will be evaluated, and state the reasons for them
3.2Analyse the points raised by people who do not accept the change, and evaluate which of them are supported by evidence
3.3Determine which points will change the department's plans and which will not, and state the reasons in each case
3.4Use relevant investigation of comparable changes, inside or outside own organisation, to inform the response
3.5Adapt the department's plans in line with the points determined at 3.3, and state what changed
3.6Determine what the department will do where a person continues not to accept the change, within the obligations and constraints identified at 1.5

Applied in Operations and service

The learner sets the criteria for judging the department's response first (3.1). A point such as a claim that the AI agent mishandles customers in vulnerable circumstances is tested against evidence (3.2). The learner decides which points change the plan (3.3). Comparable service teams inform the response (3.4), and the plan is adapted (3.5). Continued refusal is handled within 1.5 (3.6).

LO4
The learner will: Be able to work with the people whose roles change.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1State to each person whose role changes what is changing, when it changes, and what is expected of them
4.2Respond to each point raised, stating what the department will do about it and the reasons
4.3Conduct a discussion with a person who does not accept the change, and record what was agreed and what was not
4.4Determine the support each person requires to carry out the changed role, and state how and when it will be provided
4.5Determine how the department will keep the people whose roles change informed while the change proceeds, and how the effect on their work will be measured

Applied in Operations and service

Each person hears what changes, when, and what is expected, for example at a shift briefing then one-to-ones (4.1). Every point raised gets a stated response with reasons (4.2). The learner holds a recorded discussion with someone who has said they do not accept the change (4.3). Support is set per person, such as protected time off the queue (4.4). Keeping people informed and measuring the effect is planned (4.5).

LO5
The learner will: Be able to evaluate how a department worked with the people whose roles changed.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Evaluate the effect of the change on the work of the people whose roles changed, against what was determined at 4.5
5.2Evaluate the effect of the change on the department's work, using figures from the department's own systems
5.3Evaluate how far the points recorded at 2.3 changed what the department did, giving reasons
5.4Evaluate how effective the method determined at 2.2 and the criteria determined at 3.1 were, giving reasons
5.5Identify what would be determined differently at the next change to the department's roles, and the reasons

Applied in Operations and service

The learner evaluates the effect on the changed roles against 4.5 (5.1). They evaluate the effect on the department's work from its own figures (5.2). They judge how far what people raised changed what the department did (5.3). They review the method and criteria they set (5.4) and what they would determine differently (5.5).

5 learning outcomes, 27 assessment criteria. The same criteria as the generic Diploma, word for word.

Evidence from Operations and service work

  • 2.1. A role-impact list for the function, by role and not by name. It shows what changes for each role and which other teams depend on it.
  • 2.2, 2.3, 2.6. A record of how views were gathered across early, late and weekend shifts. It shows what each group raised and how absent colleagues were handled.
  • 2.4, 2.5. An analysis separating objections to the change from objections to its handling. It gives a reasoned view of which parts are least likely to hold.
  • 3.1, 3.3, 3.5. A response log with the learner's own criteria and each point raised. Each entry records the decision taken and the resulting change to the plan.
  • 4.3. A record of a discussion with Colleague A, who stated at 2.3 that they did not accept the change. It shows what was agreed and not, with witness testimony.
  • 5.1, 5.2. An evaluation of the changed roles from the department's own case, rota and quality records. It uses at least one measurement taken after the change.

Keeping it at Level 5

It drops to Level 4 when a change template or an HR briefing script fixes who to consult and what may be conceded. That decides 2.2, 3.1 and 3.3. It rises above Level 5 when the learner sets how the organisation handles role change, which is recorded at 1.5 instead.

The unit aim, level check, boundaries, assessment guidance and evidence trail are in ZFF-EI-05 on the generic Diploma, and apply here unchanged.

ZFF-AU-05

Planning Automation Across a Department

Level5TQT80 hoursCredits8GLH46 indicativeStatusMandatoryCriteria26

In Operations and service

Here the candidates are the function's own processes. Answering routine queries, routing tickets and logging complaints. Booking appointments, building rosters, processing orders and updating case records. Some are good candidates and some are not, such as complaints from customers in vulnerable circumstances. The learner works out which from the department's own figures. They consult the people affected and recommend to whoever would decide.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Know how automation changes the work of a department.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Analyse the effects that introducing automation has on the work of the people in a department
1.2Compare different approaches to introducing automation into a department, and the reasoning behind each
1.3Evaluate the reasons automation programmes fail to deliver what was expected of them
1.4Identify the constraints that limit what own department can automate, including systems, contracts, permissions and skills
1.5Evaluate the different views held within own department about automation, and the reasoning given for them

Applied in Operations and service

Advisers can lose the easy contacts that broke up a hard shift (1.1). The learner compares automating one queue at a time with one change across every channel (1.2). They evaluate why service automation disappoints, such as rising repeat contacts (1.3). Systems, supplier contracts, data permissions and the rules on this page are constraints (1.4). Views within the department are weighed (1.5).

LO2
The learner will: Be able to establish what a department does and where its effort goes.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Map the processes carried out by own department, showing inputs, outputs and the people involved
2.2Determine the method used to establish where the department's effort goes, and state the reasons for choosing it
2.3Establish the volume and the time cost of the department's main processes from the department's own systems
2.4Identify the processes that other teams depend on, and what they depend on them for
2.5Evaluate the reliability of the figures obtained, and state how gaps were handled

Applied in Operations and service

The learner maps the function's processes, inputs, outputs and people, including hand-offs (2.1). They decide how to find where effort goes, such as sampling cases, and why (2.2). Volume and time come from the department's own telephony, ticketing or order systems (2.3). They identify what other teams rely on (2.4). They judge the figures, such as miscoded contact reasons (2.5).

LO3
The learner will: Be able to evaluate processes in a department as candidates for automation.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Determine the criteria against which candidate processes will be evaluated, and state the reasons for them
3.2Analyse a candidate process to establish which parts could be automated and which could not
3.3Interpret the costs and the benefits of automating a candidate process, using figures from the department's own systems
3.4Use relevant investigation of comparable work, inside or outside own organisation, to inform the evaluation
3.5Identify a process that should not be automated, and evaluate the reasons
3.6Evaluate the candidate processes against the criteria determined at 3.1, and state which are recommended

Applied in Operations and service

The learner sets the criteria a candidate must meet before evaluating any (3.1). Each candidate is split into parts that could and could not be automated (3.2). Costs and benefits come from the department's own figures (3.3). Comparable work informs the evaluation (3.4). At least one process is kept human, with reasons (3.5). Candidates are then evaluated against the learner's criteria (3.6).

LO4
The learner will: Be able to work with the people whose work automation would change.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Identify the people whose work would change, and how it would change for each
4.2Consult those people about the proposed change, and record what was raised
4.3Analyse the concerns raised, and evaluate which of them alter the evaluation
4.4Adapt the evaluation in response to what the consultation established, and state what changed
4.5Evaluate the skills the department would need that it does not currently hold

Applied in Operations and service

The learner identifies whose work would change and how, such as advisers, quality staff and the knowledge base owner (4.1). They consult them and record what is raised (4.2). They decide which concerns alter the evaluation (4.3) and revise it (4.4). They evaluate only the skills these automations need, such as maintaining routing rules (4.5).

LO5
The learner will: Be able to recommend a course of action and evaluate own method.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1State the checks, the fallbacks and the points of human decision for each recommended process
5.2Evaluate the risks the recommendation carries for the department, and what would be done about each
5.3Present the recommendation, with the evidence, to the person who would decide
5.4Evaluate how effective the method determined at 2.2 and the criteria determined at 3.1 were, giving reasons
5.5Identify what would be determined differently in a further evaluation, and the reasons

Applied in Operations and service

Each recommended process gets checks, fallbacks and points of human decision, such as a clear route to a person (5.1). Risks to the department are evaluated, each with a response (5.2). The recommendation goes to the person who would decide (5.3). The learner reviews the method and criteria they set (5.4) and what they would change (5.5).

5 learning outcomes, 26 assessment criteria. The same criteria as the generic Diploma, word for word.

Evidence from Operations and service work

  • 2.1, 2.4. A process map of the function, from contact or order received to case closed. It shows inputs, outputs, roles and the teams that depend on each step.
  • 2.2, 2.3, 2.5. A method note and an effort table from the team's own queue and ticket data. Notes record miscoded or missing records.
  • 3.1, 3.2, 3.6. An evaluation of candidate processes against the learner's own criteria. Each process is split into parts that could and could not be automated.
  • 3.5. A reasoned case for keeping one process human. For example, handling complaints from customers in vulnerable circumstances.
  • 4.2, 4.3, 4.4. Consultation notes from advisers, team leaders and the knowledge base owner, by role. A dated revision shows how the evaluation changed.
  • 5.1, 5.2, 5.3. The recommendation as presented, with checks, fallbacks and human decision points for each process. A risk table and witness testimony of the presentation.

Keeping it at Level 5

It drops to Level 4 when the learner is told which queues to automate, or given a supplier's business case template or a cost per contact target. Any one decides 2.2 or 3.1. It rises above Level 5 when it reshapes the organisation's channel strategy, which is recorded at 1.4 instead.

ZFF-DA-05

Using Data to Direct a Department's Priorities

Level5TQT70 hoursCredits7GLH40 indicativeStatusMandatoryCriteria25

In Operations and service

Operations and service departments produce a lot of data. Queue and wait times, contact reasons, handle times and resolution rates. Complaint categories, order records, field visit outcomes and quality scores. Many of these measures were set long ago and drive behaviour nobody chose. The learner works out what the measures count and encourage. Then they use the data to decide where effort should go.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Know what a department's measures show and what they drive.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Analyse what the measures reported by own department actually count, and over what period
1.2Analyse the behaviour each measure encourages in the people whose work it reports on
1.3Evaluate what own department's current measures leave out
1.4Compare different approaches to measuring work of this kind, and the reasoning behind each
1.5Evaluate the different views held within own department about what its measures show, and the reasoning given for them

Applied in Operations and service

Does a resolved ticket mean the customer stopped contacting, or the adviser closed it (1.1)? The learner analyses what each measure drives, such as rushing calls to protect handle time (1.2). They evaluate what the measures miss, such as repeat contact on another channel (1.3). They compare ways of measuring service work (1.4). They weigh views about what the figures show (1.5).

LO2
The learner will: Be able to determine a question about a department's priorities that data could help settle.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Determine the question about own department's priorities that the work will address, and state the reasons for selecting it
2.2Determine the data that bears on the question, and state the reasons for the selection
2.3Identify data that was available but set aside, and evaluate the effect of setting it aside
2.4Determine the method to be used to work with the data, and state the reasons for choosing it
2.5Evaluate the quality of the data obtained, and state how gaps and errors were handled

Applied in Operations and service

The learner decides the question, for example whether effort goes into contacts the department's own processes create (2.1). They choose the data that bears on it (2.2). They state what was set aside and its effect (2.3). They decide how to work with the data (2.4). They judge its quality, including miscoded reasons and cases closed in bulk (2.5).

LO3
The learner will: Be able to analyse a department's data and interpret what it indicates.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Analyse the selected data in relation to the question
3.2Interpret what the analysis indicates about where the department's effort is going
3.3Identify an interpretation the same data would also support, and evaluate which of the two it better supports
3.4Use relevant investigation, inside or outside own organisation, to test whether the interpretation holds
3.5Evaluate the limits of what the data can show, and what would be needed to settle the question
3.6Identify where an AI or automated tool was used in the analysis, and evaluate what was checked and why

Applied in Operations and service

The learner analyses the data against the question (3.1) and interprets where effort goes (3.2). They name a second reading, such as seasonal demand rather than a process fault, and judge between them (3.3). Comparable work tests the reading (3.4). The limits of the data are stated (3.5). Where an AI tool categorised contacts, the learner says what was checked (3.6).

LO4
The learner will: Be able to direct a department's priorities from what data indicates.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Determine the changes to the department's priorities that follow from the interpretation
4.2Evaluate what the department would stop or reduce in order to make the changes possible
4.3Consult the people whose work the changes would affect, and record what was raised
4.4Adapt the proposed changes in response to what the consultation established, and state what changed
4.5Present the proposed priorities, with the evidence, to the person who decides them, and respond to challenge
4.6State how the effect of the changes will be measured, and over what period

Applied in Operations and service

The learner decides the changes to priorities that follow (4.1). They decide what the department would stop or reduce to make room (4.2). They consult the people affected (4.3) and adapt the changes (4.4). They present to the person who sets the department's priorities and answer challenge (4.5). They state how the effect will be measured (4.6).

LO5
The learner will: Be able to evaluate the effect of directing priorities from data.
3 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Evaluate the effect of the changed priorities against what was stated at 4.6, using evidence
5.2Evaluate how effective the method determined at 2.4 was, giving reasons
5.3Identify what the department would measure differently, and what would be determined differently next time, and the reasons

Applied in Operations and service

The learner evaluates the effect against what was stated at 4.6 (5.1). They review the method set at 2.4 (5.2). They identify what the department would measure differently, and what they would determine differently next time (5.3).

5 learning outcomes, 25 assessment criteria. The same criteria as the generic Diploma, word for word.

Evidence from Operations and service work

  • 1.1, 1.2, 1.3. An annotated list of the function's current measures. For each, what it counts, the behaviour it drives on the floor and what it misses.
  • 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4. A question and method note. It names the data chosen from the team's own case and contact records, the data set aside, and why.
  • 2.5, 3.5. A data quality note on miscoded contact reasons, duplicates and gaps. It states what the data cannot show.
  • 3.3, 3.6. An analysis comparing two readings of the same queue data. It declares any AI categorisation used and the sample checked by hand.
  • 4.3, 4.5. Consultation notes by role. Witness testimony of the presentation to the person who sets the priorities, with the challenge and the response.
  • 5.1. A follow-up using at least one measurement taken after the change, against the measure stated at 4.6. It states its period and limits.

Keeping it at Level 5

It drops to Level 4 when the learner is given the question, or a dashboard and service-level target that already decide which figures matter. 2.1 and 2.4 must be theirs. It rises above Level 5 when the learner reconsiders what the department measures for, or sets organisation-wide service standards.

The unit aim, level check, boundaries, assessment guidance and evidence trail are in ZFF-DA-05 on the generic Diploma, and apply here unchanged.

ZFF-PJ-05

Applied Project: Annual Automation Plan for Own Department

Level5TQT140 hoursCredits14GLH10 indicativeStatusMandatoryCriteria30

In Operations and service

The plan covers one function's year. Seasonal peaks, the quarter-end order surge, annual renewals and weather that drives field service demand. Audits, and the processes that appear only once a year. The learner sets the boundary, maps and costs the work, and chooses what to automate and what to keep human. They consult, sequence the changes around the peaks, and present the plan for sign-off.

Learning outcomes and assessment criteria

LO1
The learner will: Be able to establish what own department does and what it costs.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
1.1Determine the boundary of the department the plan will cover, and state the reasons for it
1.2Map the processes the department carries out across a year, including those that occur only occasionally
1.3Establish the volume, the time and the cost of each main process from the department's own systems
1.4Determine the method used to establish those figures, and state the reasons for choosing it
1.5Evaluate the reliability of the figures, and state how gaps and disputed figures were handled
1.6Identify the obligations and commitments the department must continue to meet whatever the plan changes

Applied in Operations and service

The learner sets the boundary, such as customer service with complaints but not the warehouse, and why (1.1). They map the year, including rare processes such as a product recall (1.2). Volume, time and cost come from the department's own systems (1.3), by a method they choose (1.4). Disputed figures are resolved and recorded (1.5). Fixed obligations, such as client contract commitments, are identified (1.6).

LO2
The learner will: Be able to analyse which of a department's processes are candidates for automation.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
2.1Determine the criteria by which candidate processes will be selected, and state the reasons for them
2.2Analyse each main process against those criteria
2.3Interpret the cost and the benefit of automating each candidate, using the department's own figures
2.4Use relevant investigation of comparable work to inform the evaluation, and state what it established
2.5Identify the processes that should not be automated, and evaluate the reasons for each
2.6Evaluate the candidates against one another and state the order in which they are recommended

Applied in Operations and service

The learner sets the selection criteria (2.1) and analyses each main process against them (2.2). Each candidate is costed from the department's own figures (2.3). Comparable work informs the evaluation, with what it established (2.4). Processes to keep human are named with reasons (2.5). Candidates are ranked against one another (2.6).

LO3
The learner will: Be able to consult the people whose work a plan would change.
5 criteria
RefThe learner can
3.1Identify the people whose work each recommended change would affect, and how it would affect them
3.2Consult those people, and record what was raised
3.3Analyse the concerns raised and the reasoning given for them, and evaluate which of them change the plan
3.4Adapt the plan in response, and state what changed and the reasons
3.5Evaluate the skills the department will need that it does not currently hold, and state how they will be obtained

Applied in Operations and service

The learner identifies who each change would affect, including other shifts, sites and dependent teams (3.1). They consult them and record what is raised (3.2). They analyse the concerns and decide which change the plan (3.3). The plan is adapted with reasons (3.4). The skills this plan needs, and how to obtain them, are evaluated (3.5).

LO4
The learner will: Be able to produce a sequenced annual plan with checks and fallbacks.
7 criteria
RefThe learner can
4.1Sequence the recommended changes across the year, and state the reasons for the order
4.2Identify the dependencies between the changes, and between the changes and work outside the department
4.3State the resources each change requires, and when they are required
4.4State the checks that will be carried out on each change, by whom, and at what point
4.5State the fallback for each change, and the point at which the fallback would be used
4.6Evaluate the risks the plan carries for the department, and state what would be done about each
4.7Determine how the effect of each change will be measured, and against what starting figure

Applied in Operations and service

Changes are sequenced around the department's own year, such as no go-live before a known peak (4.1). Dependencies on IT, suppliers and other departments are identified (4.2). Resources and timing are stated (4.3). Each change has checks and owners (4.4) and a fallback, such as reopening a human queue (4.5). Risks are evaluated (4.6), and each change has a starting figure (4.7).

LO5
The learner will: Be able to present a departmental plan and evaluate own method.
6 criteria
RefThe learner can
5.1Present the plan to the person who signs off the department's plans, in a form suited to that decision
5.2Respond to challenge on the plan's figures, its sequence and its risks
5.3Record the decision taken and any conditions attached to it
5.4Evaluate how effective the method determined at 1.4 and the criteria determined at 2.1 were, giving reasons
5.5Evaluate how far the consultation changed the plan, giving reasons
5.6Identify what would be determined differently in the next annual plan, and the reasons

Applied in Operations and service

The plan goes to the person who signs off the department's plans (5.1). The learner answers challenge on figures, sequence and risks (5.2). The decision and any conditions are recorded (5.3). They evaluate their method and criteria (5.4) and how far consultation changed the plan (5.5). They identify what they would determine differently next year (5.6).

5 learning outcomes, 30 assessment criteria. The same criteria as the generic Diploma, word for word.

Evidence from Operations and service work

  • 1.1, 1.2. A boundary statement and a year map of the function's processes. It marks the peaks and the occasional processes found in a full year of records.
  • 1.3, 1.4, 1.5. A costed process table from the department's own telephony, ticketing, order or job records. A method note shows how disputed figures were resolved.
  • 2.1, 2.5, 2.6. A ranked candidate evaluation against the learner's own criteria. It names the processes kept human and the reasons for each.
  • 3.2, 3.3, 3.4. A consultation record across shifts and sites, by role. A change log shows how the plan moved in response.
  • 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, 4.7. The annual plan itself, sequenced around the peaks. It shows outside dependencies, checks, fallbacks and a starting figure for each measure.
  • 5.1, 5.2, 5.3. The presentation pack and witness testimony of the challenge raised and answered. The recorded decision, with any conditions.

Keeping it at Level 5

It drops to Level 4 when the learner is given the process list, the criteria, a benefits template or an efficiency target. It rises above Level 5 when the plan redesigns how the organisation serves its customers. A needed organisational change is recorded at 4.2 as a dependency instead.

The unit aim, level check, boundaries, assessment guidance and evidence trail are in ZFF-PJ-05 on the generic Diploma, and apply here unchanged.

Section 5

Assessment

This version is assessed exactly as the generic Diploma: by portfolio from real work, decided by a human assessor, with a recorded professional discussion for every unit. See assessment and quality assurance and the evidence trail on the generic Diploma.

Section 6

What we know is not yet right

Listed plainly, so that a reviewer has this list before finding any of it.

1

No operations or service practitioner, and no assessor, has read this version yet. The examples follow the descriptor and the generic units. They have not been tested against a real department.

2

The rules list is a starting set for UK employers. Sector rules for service teams in utilities, telecoms, housing or health are not covered. They would need checking for a learner in those sectors.

3

Shift-based teams may find it hard to consult every shift (EI-05 2.3 and 4.3, PJ-05 3.2). Whether consultation sampled by shift is enough is for an assessor to confirm.

4

Everything open on the generic Diploma applies here too. See its open items.
